title: How to Sell Ebooks and Guides Online in 2026
excerpt: Learn how to sell ebooks and guides online in 2026: write a focused book, pick the right format and store, set a fair price, and reach readers who need it.
coverAlt: An ebook author holding a finished guide ready for online sale
haystack:
how to sell ebooks and guides online in 2026 learn how to sell ebooks and guides online in 2026: write a focused book, pick the right format and store, set a fair price, and reach readers who need it. digital-products ebooks self publishing digital products an ebook is a book a reader can buy and read within minutes, on a phone, tablet, or e-reader. for a beginner, it is one of the most accessible digital products: it needs writing skill, not design software or video equipment, and it can be sold on large stores or directly from your own page. but ebooks also compete with millions of other titles, and a book that tries to cover everything usually sells less well than a short book that solves one problem clearly.

this guide covers ebooks and guides only: choosing a focused topic, writing a book readers finish, formatting it, choosing where to sell it, understanding royalties honestly, and reaching your first readers. it does not cover templates or courses in depth, which have their own guides, and it only touches pricing briefly. read the pricing guide before you set a final price.

## choose a focused topic readers already want

a good ebook topic sits at the meeting point of three things: a problem readers already search for, knowledge you genuinely have, and a result you can deliver in a short book. start with problems, as with any first product. look at questions people ask repeatedly in communities, comments, and search suggestions. a topic with existing books is a good sign: it proves readers buy books on the subject. your job is not to invent a new subject, but to serve a specific reader better than existing books do.

narrow the reader and the promise. "a guide to fitness" will compete with thousands of titles. "a twelve week strength plan for busy parents who train at home with dumbbells" names a reader, a situation, and a result. narrow books are easier to title, easier to describe, and easier for a reader to choose. they also earn better reviews, because the right reader gets exactly what was promised.

## write a short book readers actually finish

most first ebooks fail by being too long and too general. a reader buys a guide to solve a problem, not to admire its length. aim for a book that a reader can finish in a few sittings: for most practical guides, that means roughly 15,000 to 30,000 words, or about 60 to 120 pages. shorter is fine if the problem is narrow. a 40 page guide that a reader completes and uses beats a 200 page book that a reader abandons at chapter two.

structure the book around the reader's journey. open with the problem and the promise, then move step by step toward the result, in the order the reader will act. give each chapter one job, and end each chapter with a clear next action. use headings, short paragraphs, lists, and tables where they help, because guides are read for use, not only for reading. include examples from real situations you know, described honestly, and avoid invented stories or results. a worked example with realistic numbers teaches more than a vague success story.

## format the book properly

formatting is the step that separates a professional ebook from a document that happens to be sold. readers notice bad formatting immediately: broken paragraphs, missing chapter breaks, images that do not fit the screen, and tables that overflow. good formatting is mostly invisible, and that is the point.

the two main ebook formats serve different purposes. epub is the standard for most ebook stores and e-readers, because it reflows: the text adjusts to the reader's screen size and font choice. pdf keeps an exact layout, which suits workbooks, planners, and guides where design and page position matter, but it reads poorly on small phone screens. many authors sell both: epub for reading, pdf for workbooks or for direct sales where the buyer prints pages.

| format | best for | reads well on | watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| epub | standard guides and nonfiction | e-readers, tablets, phones, most stores | test on a real device, not only in preview software |
| mobi or kfx | amazon kindle delivery | kindle devices and apps | amazon converts your file; check the converted result |
| pdf | workbooks, planners, designed guides | computers, tablets, print | poor on small phones; keep file size reasonable |
| paperback via print on demand | readers who prefer print | physical book | needs a print ready interior and cover; proof copy first |

![ebook formats compared for reading and selling](/covers/ebook-formats.jpg)

## choose where to sell: stores, direct, or both

you have three main routes, and many authors use more than one. each route trades reach against control and income per sale, so the right choice depends on your goals and your audience.

amazon kindle direct publishing, known as kdp, gives you access to the largest ebook store and to kindle readers worldwide. you upload your manuscript and cover, set a price, and amazon handles delivery, payment, and much of the discovery through search and recommendations. the trade is control: amazon sets the store rules, takes its share, and can change terms. kdp also offers optional exclusivity programmes with extra promotion tools, but exclusivity means you cannot sell the same ebook elsewhere during the term, so read those terms carefully before enrolling.

selling direct, from your own page through a platform such as gumroad or payhip, gives you more income per sale, your buyers' contact details, and full control over price and presentation. the trade is traffic: nobody finds your page unless you bring them there. direct sales suit authors who already have an audience, an email list, or a community. other ebook stores and distributors widen your reach beyond amazon without exclusivity, but each store has its own rules and usually smaller traffic than amazon, so weigh the setup effort against realistic sales.

## understand royalties honestly, including a real conflict

royalties are the share of each sale you keep, and they vary by store, price, and programme. this is an area where beginners get misled by confident claims, so read this section carefully and check the live pages before you price.

for kdp specifically, published guides conflict on the royalty price band, and you should know about the conflict rather than trusting a single figure. older guides say the higher royalty rate applies to ebooks priced from $2.99 to $9.99. guides published in october 2026 say the band is $2.99 to $12.99. the band has changed, and the older figure still circulates widely, so neither figure should be treated as settled fact from a guide alone. before you price your book, check the live kdp pricing page and read the current royalty terms for your country and format. price your book based on what the live page says on the day you publish, not on what any guide, including this one, reports second hand.

![ebook selling routes and royalty paths compared](/covers/ebook-royalty-routes.jpg)

the same caution applies to every platform. fees, royalty shares, delivery costs, and tax handling differ by store and change over time. before you commit to a route, read the live fee and royalty page of each platform you consider, and work out what you keep per sale at your planned price after all deductions. a price that looks good before fees can be disappointing after them, and a royalty rate that applies in one country or price band may not apply in another. the pricing guide on this site shows the calculation method; the live platform pages supply the current numbers.

## reach your first readers

a book without readers is a file, not a product. launch planning should start while you write, not after you publish. build a simple launch list: people who asked about the topic, community members who followed your writing, and readers of any free content you shared. a short free sample chapter, offered in exchange for an email address, is a fair trade and gives you a list of people who already want the topic.

at launch, tell your list first, then share the book where your readers gather, with a clear description of who it is for and what result it delivers. ask early readers, politely and without pressure, to leave an honest review if they found the book useful. reviews matter enormously in ebook stores: they influence search visibility and buyer trust. never buy reviews, never write your own reviews under another name, and never offer payment for positive reviews. honest reviews from real readers are slower to collect and far more valuable.

after launch, keep the book visible with useful content about its topic: short articles, answers to reader questions, and updated editions when the subject changes. a second edition notice gives past readers a reason to return and new readers a reason to trust that the book is maintained. if sales are slow, treat that as information: check whether the cover, title, description, or price is the problem, and change one thing at a time. many books find their readers gradually through search and recommendations rather than in a launch week spike.

## risks and limits

ebook income is uneven and usually modest at first. stores are crowded, search visibility takes time, and a book on a fast changing topic can become outdated. returns and refunds happen, store rules change, and a book that depends on one store is exposed if that store changes its terms. keep costs low, do not borrow to fund a first book, and do not present a first ebook as a reliable income replacement.

results vary with topic, competition, cover, description, price, reviews, and how consistently you promote the book. avoid income claims from sellers that promise specific earnings, and do not make such claims about your own book. a first ebook that helps real readers, earns honest reviews, and grows a small reader list is a genuine success and a base for the next book.

## frequently asked questions

### do i need an isbn to sell an ebook?
not always. amazon kdp assigns its own identifier and does not require you to buy an isbn for ebooks sold there. other stores and distributors may handle identifiers differently, and print editions have separate requirements. check the rules of each store you plan to use before you publish, and decide whether owning your own isbn matters for your wider distribution plans.

### what is the best format for selling ebooks?
epub is the best general choice for reading on most devices and stores, while pdf suits workbooks and designed guides. many authors offer both, choosing per route: epub for stores, pdf for direct sales or printable companions. test every format on a real device before launch.

### how much royalty do ebook authors earn?
it depends on the store, the price, the country, and the programme, and published figures conflict, as explained above for the kdp price band. check the live royalty page of each platform at publication time and calculate what you keep per sale after fees and delivery costs, rather than trusting a single quoted rate.

### how do i market an ebook with no audience?
share useful content on the book's topic where your readers gather, offer a free sample chapter for an email address, and collect honest reviews from early readers. expect gradual growth through search and recommendations, and build your reader list with every book so the next launch starts stronger.

### should i sell on amazon, direct, or both?
amazon gives reach, direct sales give control and more income per sale, and many authors use both. start with the route that matches your current audience: kdp for discovery if you have no audience, direct sales if you already have buyers, and add the other route once the first one works.

## your next step

your next step is to write one paragraph naming your reader, their problem, and the result your book will deliver. if that paragraph is clear, outline the chapters in the order the reader will act, and write the first chapter this week. if the paragraph is vague, narrow the reader before you write another word.

for the wider journey, read [how to create your first digital product in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-create-your-first-digital-product) if you have not yet validated an idea, and read [how to price digital products in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-price-digital-products) before you set a final price. for other product types, see [how to sell templates online in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-sell-templates-online) and [how to create and sell an online course in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-create-and-sell-an-online-course). if you are still shaping the business around the book, read [how to start an online business as a beginner in 2026](/online-business/how-to-start-online-business-beginner) and [online business models explained: which one fits you in 2026](/online-business/online-business-models-explained).

title: How to Create and Sell an Online Course in 2026
excerpt: Learn how to create and sell an online course in 2026: plan a focused curriculum, record with simple gear, price it well, and launch to your first students.
coverAlt: An online course creator recording a lesson at a simple home desk setup
haystack:
how to create and sell an online course in 2026 learn how to create and sell an online course in 2026: plan a focused curriculum, record with simple gear, price it well, and launch to your first students. digital-products online courses course creation digital products an online course is a digital product with a promise bigger than a template or a guide: by the end, the student can do something they could not do before. that promise is why courses can charge more, and also why they fail more visibly. a course that teaches everything about a topic but changes nothing for the student will not earn repeat sales or good reviews. a focused course that takes a beginner to one clear result will.

this guide covers courses only: choosing a result worth teaching, planning a curriculum, recording with simple equipment, choosing a platform, launching to your first students, and supporting them well. it does not cover templates or ebooks in depth, which have their own guides, and it only touches pricing briefly. read the pricing guide before you set a final price.

## start with the result, not the topic

most first courses fail at the planning stage because the creator starts with a topic instead of a result. "social media marketing" is a topic, and a course on it could run for twenty hours and still leave a student unsure what to do. "plan and publish your first month of content for a small business instagram account" is a result. a student knows whether they achieved it, and a buyer knows whether they want it.

define your result in one sentence that names the student, the starting point, and the finish line. for example: "a beginner freelancer who has never pitched will send five tailored pitches by the end of the course." then list the skills that result requires, in the order the student needs them. that list becomes your curriculum. anything that does not serve the result is cut, however interesting it is. a short course that delivers its promise beats a long course that wanders.

## plan a curriculum students can finish

completion matters more than comprehensiveness. students who finish a course recommend it, review it, and buy the next one. students who stall at lesson three do none of those things. design for finishing: short lessons, clear progress, and a small win in every module.

a practical structure for a first course is four to six modules, each with three to six lessons, each lesson five to twelve minutes long. open with a module that gives a quick, visible win, such as setting up the tool or completing the first small task. put the hardest material in the middle, when students are already invested, and close with a module where students apply everything to their own project. end every module with one action step, written plainly: "by the end of this module, you will have drafted your first three post ideas." action steps turn watching into doing, and doing is what produces results.

![a course curriculum planned around one clear student outcome](/covers/course-curriculum.jpg)

## validate the course before you record it all

recording a full course before anyone wants it is the most expensive mistake a first course creator can make. validate first, using the same principle as any first product: check that strangers want the result before you build the whole thing.

a simple validation route is a presell or beta launch. outline the course, write the sales page, and offer a small number of founding student places at a lower price, with the honest explanation that the course is being recorded now and students will get early access plus input on the content. if enough people join, you have both proof and your first students. if almost nobody joins after you shared it in relevant places, you have learned something valuable before spending weeks recording.

a beta group also improves the course itself. your first students will ask the questions your outline missed, stumble where your instructions are unclear, and tell you which lessons felt too long. record with their feedback in mind, and you will launch a stronger course than one recorded in isolation. treat beta students well: answer their questions promptly, credit their help, and give them the finished course and future updates. their testimonials, given honestly and with permission, become your best sales material.

## record with simple gear and a clean process

you do not need a studio to record a good course. you need clear audio, readable visuals, and a quiet room. audio matters most: students forgive an ordinary picture, but they abandon a course they cannot hear comfortably. a decent usb microphone, a quiet room with soft furnishings to reduce echo, and a short test recording checked on headphones will beat an expensive camera with bad sound.

editing should be light but real: remove long pauses, mistakes, and filler, add chapter markers or section titles, and check that every lesson's audio level matches. export at a quality the platform recommends, and watch each finished lesson once from start to finish before publishing. students judge a course by its rough edges, and a lesson with a frozen screen or missing audio will damage trust even if the content is good.

| course element | simple approach for a first course | avoid |
|---|---|---|
| audio | usb microphone, quiet room, test recording | built in laptop microphone in a noisy room |
| video | screen recording plus short talking head parts | long unedited takes with no visual change |
| lesson length | 5 to 12 minutes, one idea per lesson | 45 minute lectures with several ideas mixed |
| materials | one worksheet or checklist per module | a large file dump with no guidance |
| support | email or community replies within two days | no contact route and no response times stated |

## choose a platform that fits how you sell

course platforms fall into two broad groups. hosted course platforms such as teachable, thinkific, and podia handle video hosting, student accounts, checkout, and progress tracking, and they charge a subscription, a transaction fee, or both. general selling platforms such as gumroad handle checkout and delivery but offer simpler course features. marketplaces bring their own buyers but take a larger share and control pricing and promotion more tightly.

choose based on how you will reach students. if you already have an audience and want control over price and branding, a hosted platform or your own site with a course plugin suits you. if you have no audience and want discovery, a marketplace can bring students, but expect less control and a smaller share per sale. if you are testing a first course, a simple platform with low fixed costs is wiser than an expensive plan you must grow into.

fees and terms change, so check each platform's live pricing and fee page before you commit, and calculate what you keep per sale at your planned price. also check practical details: can students download lessons, does the platform handle tax collection for you, can you offer coupons and payment plans, and can you export your student list if you move later. your student list is an asset; a platform that locks it away is a risk to your future launches.

## launch to your first students

a course launch works best as a short, planned sequence, not a single announcement. start with the people who validated the idea: your waitlist, your beta students, and the communities where you tested the concept. tell them when enrolment opens, what the course includes, what result it delivers, and when the launch price ends. a launch window of one to two weeks gives people time to decide without letting the announcement fade.

during launch week, teach in public. share a free lesson, a useful tip, or a worked example that shows your teaching style and gives real value even to people who do not buy. answer questions openly, including hard ones about who the course is not for. honest answers build more trust than hype, and a buyer who knows the course fits them is far less likely to refund.

![a launch plan for a first online course](/covers/course-launch-plan.jpg)

## support students and protect your reputation

student support is part of the product, not an extra. state your support route and response time on the course page, and keep it. a student who waits a week for an answer will assume the course is abandoned. answer in batches if needed, but answer reliably. keep a list of repeated questions and turn them into a course faq or an added lesson. each addition makes the course better for the next group.

set fair boundaries. you support the course material and the stated result, not each student's entire business or unlimited one to one coaching, unless coaching is explicitly included and priced. if a student needs personal help beyond the course, you may offer it as a separate service or point them to the relevant lesson. clear boundaries, stated kindly, protect both the student and your time.

refunds deserve a clear, fair policy stated before purchase, such as a set number of days with reasonable conditions. a fair refund policy increases buyer confidence and reduces disputes. handle refund requests promptly and politely, even when you disagree. one graceful refund costs less than a public complaint from a frustrated buyer.

## risks and limits

courses take longer to build than templates or short guides, and the return is uncertain until students enrol. recording, editing, platform fees, and support all cost time or money, and a course on a fast changing tool may need regular updates. sales can also be uneven: launches spike, then enrolment slows until the next push. do not borrow money or quit stable work to fund a first course, and keep your fixed costs low until enrolment proves itself.

results vary with your topic, your audience, your teaching quality, your price, and how consistently you promote the course. avoid income claims you cannot support, and be cautious about claims from course sellers about their own earnings. a first course that helps twenty students reach a real result, earns honest reviews, and teaches you how to teach is a genuine success, whatever the revenue. build on that foundation with a second course or an improved version, rather than chasing a large launch before you are ready.

## frequently asked questions

### how long should my first online course be?
long enough to deliver one clear result and no longer. for most first courses, that means two to four hours of video across four to six modules, plus worksheets. a shorter course that students finish beats a longer course that students abandon.

### what equipment do i need to record a course?
a decent usb microphone, a quiet room, screen recording software, and a computer that can handle recording and editing. a phone or basic webcam is enough for talking head parts at first. spend on audio before video, and test everything with a short sample lesson before recording the full course.

### how do i get students without an audience?
validate with a beta group, share useful teaching content where your buyers gather, and consider a marketplace that brings its own buyers. expect slower early enrolment, and build an email list from every free lesson and launch so your second course starts with an audience your first course created.

### should i presell my course before recording it?
preselling is a sensible test if you are honest about the timeline and deliver what you promised. it proves demand before you spend weeks recording, and it gives you founding students whose feedback improves the course. do not presell a course you are not committed to finishing on schedule.

### how much should i charge for my first course?
first courses often start in a low to mid double figure range, with the exact price depending on the result, the depth, and the support included. those are starter ranges only. read the full pricing guide on this site and check each platform's live fee page before you set a final price.

## your next step

your next step is to write one sentence naming your student, their starting point, and the result your course will deliver. if you cannot write that sentence, your course idea is not ready to outline yet. once you can, list the skills the result requires, validate the idea with a beta offer, and record one module at a time.

for the wider journey, read [how to create your first digital product in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-create-your-first-digital-product) if you have not yet validated an idea, and read [how to price digital products in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-price-digital-products) before you set a final price. for other product types, see [how to sell templates online in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-sell-templates-online) and [how to sell ebooks and guides online in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-sell-ebooks-online). if you are still shaping the business around the course, read [how to start an online business as a beginner in 2026](/online-business/how-to-start-online-business-beginner) and [how to validate a business idea in 2026 before you spend money](/online-business/how-to-validate-business-idea).

title: How to Sell Templates Online in 2026
excerpt: Learn how to sell templates online in 2026: choose a format buyers want, build a strong listing, price your first pack, and handle support without burning out.
coverAlt: A collection of clean, ready to use templates displayed for online sale
haystack:
how to sell templates online in 2026 learn how to sell templates online in 2026: choose a format buyers want, build a strong listing, price your first pack, and handle support without burning out. digital-products templates selling templates digital products templates are one of the simplest digital products to sell, because the buyer understands the value in seconds. a resume template, a budget spreadsheet, a content calendar, or a set of social media designs promises a faster result than starting from a blank page. that clarity is your advantage, but it also means competition is strong. to sell templates, you need a useful template, a listing that shows it clearly, and a price that matches what buyers already expect.

this guide covers templates only: which formats sell, how to build a template buyers can actually use, how to list it, how to license it, and how to support it without spending your life on emails. it does not cover courses or ebooks, which have their own guides on this site, and it only gives starter price ranges. full pricing method is in the pricing guide linked below.

## what buyers want from a template

a buyer does not buy a template for its beauty alone. they buy it to skip work. the best templates remove decisions: the structure is done, the labels are clear, the example content shows how it should look, and the instructions say what to do first. a beautiful template that confuses its buyer will get refunds and bad reviews. a plain template that works in five minutes will get repeat buyers.

## choose a format that fits the task

different tasks suit different formats, and the format decides where you can sell and what buyers expect. pick the format your buyers already use. if your buyers plan in notion, a pdf planner will not help them, however good it looks. if your buyers design in canva, a photoshop file excludes them.

| format | best for | buyer needs | watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| notion template | planning, tracking, content systems | a free or paid notion account | duplication steps must be clear; test the duplicate link |
| canva template | social posts, presentations, planners | a free or paid canva account | check which elements are free versus paid in canva |
| spreadsheet (sheets or excel) | budgets, trackers, calculators | sheets or excel | formulas must work in both; test on mobile |
| document template | resumes, letters, planners, worksheets | word, docs, or pages | fonts must be common or embedded; check page breaks |
| social media template pack | posts, stories, covers | canva or design software | sizes must match current platform specs; check before launch |

notion and canva templates are popular first products because buyers already live in those tools and sharing is simple. spreadsheet templates suit tracking tasks where calculation matters. document templates suit anything a buyer prints or sends, such as resumes and invoices. social template packs suit creators and small businesses that post often and want a consistent look.

## build a template buyers can use in minutes

start with one use case and one user. "a content calendar for solo creators who post three times a week" is buildable. "a content system for everyone" is not. list the exact tasks your buyer does, then design the template around those tasks in the order they do them. if a step is missing, the buyer stalls. if a step is confusing, the buyer emails you.

build the template, then test it as a stranger. duplicate it, open it fresh, and complete the task using only what is inside the file. note every moment of confusion and fix it. add a short start page or instruction sheet: what the template is for, how to copy or duplicate it, what to change first, and where to get help. keep instructions short and visual where possible. a two minute video walkthrough, even recorded on a phone, can prevent many support emails, though it is optional for a first template.

## write a listing that shows the product

on a marketplace, your listing does the selling. buyers scroll quickly, compare options, and click the listing that looks most useful. your listing must answer three questions in seconds: what is this, who is it for, and what does it look like inside.

the preview images matter more than any other part of the listing. show the template itself, not a decorative graphic about it. include a full view of the main page, a close view of a key section, and a view showing example content filled in. if the template has multiple pages, show the best three or four. use clean mockups that look like the real product, and do not use screenshots of someone else's work or stock images that misrepresent what the buyer receives.

![a template listing preview showing the inside pages a buyer will receive](/covers/template-listing-preview.jpg)

the title should name the product and its user in plain words, such as "freelancer budget spreadsheet for google sheets." the description should open with the problem and the result, then list exactly what is included: number of pages or sheets, file formats, tools required, and whether updates are included. end with practical details: how delivery works, what licence the buyer receives, and your support and refund policy. honest details build trust, and trust converts browsers into buyers.

## price your first template pack

template buyers compare prices quickly, because similar templates sit side by side on marketplaces. a first template usually sells in a low range: single templates often sit at low single figures, and small packs at low double figures. those are starter ranges only, not rules. the full method for choosing a price, including fees, value, and tiers, is in the pricing guide on this site, and you should read it before setting a final price.

three pricing habits help beginners. first, check live fee pages before you price. marketplaces and payment processors charge transaction fees, payment processing fees, and sometimes listing fees, and those fees change. a price that looks fine before fees can become unprofitable after them. second, price the pack, not just the page count. a ten page template that saves a buyer an hour is worth more than a fifty page template that saves nobody any time. third, start at a price that lets strangers say yes easily, then raise it as reviews and proof accumulate. early sales and reviews are worth more than a high price with no sales.

## licence, ownership, and protecting your work

a licence tells the buyer what they may do with the template. most template sellers offer a personal licence: the buyer may use it for their own projects but may not resell, share, or give it away. some sellers offer a commercial licence at a higher price, allowing use in client work. write your licence in plain language on the listing and inside the download. state clearly what is allowed, what is not, and what happens with client work. plain language prevents most disputes.

you cannot fully prevent copying or sharing, and worrying about it excessively will slow you down. practical protections help: add a small credit line inside the file, use your shop name in file names, and include a licence note in the download. watermarking the preview images (not the delivered file) also helps, because it stops people using your listing images as the product itself. if you find your template resold, report it through the marketplace's process with proof of your original files and dates. keep your source files and creation dates as evidence.

also respect other creators' rights in your own work. do not include fonts, photos, icons, or graphics you do not have the right to resell. use your own designs or assets with a licence that explicitly allows use inside products for resale. this is not just a legal point; marketplaces remove listings built on unlicensed assets, and a removal can cost you ranking and reviews you worked hard to earn.

## support without burning out

support is where many template sellers quietly burn out, because every buyer question feels urgent and every message interrupts building. a good support routine protects your time and still treats buyers well. start with prevention: a clear instruction sheet, a short faq inside the download, and a listing that states exactly what tools and versions the template needs. most support questions come from missing information, not from difficult buyers.

set a support promise you can keep, such as replies within two working days by email, and state it on the listing. answer in batches once or twice a day instead of reacting to every message instantly. keep a document of repeated questions and turn the answers into an updated instruction sheet. each update reduces future messages. for genuinely broken files, fix fast and apologise plainly; a quick fix often turns an unhappy buyer into a positive reviewer.

![common template formats side by side for comparison](/covers/template-formats.jpg)

know the boundary of your support. you support the template working as described, not the buyer's whole business, their software training, or custom redesigns. if a buyer asks for custom work, you may offer it as a separate paid service or decline politely and point them to the instructions. a clear boundary, stated kindly, is fair to both sides and keeps a small shop sustainable.

## risks and limits

template income varies widely. some niches are crowded, and standing out takes time, good previews, and reviews. platform rules and fees change, search rankings shift, and a template built for one tool version may need updating when that tool changes. sales can be seasonal: resume templates rise when hiring rises, planner templates rise at the start of a year. plan for uneven months rather than assuming steady daily sales.

do not promise income results you cannot guarantee. a template that helps a buyer organise their work is a real, honest product even if it never earns a large income. treat your first template as a low cost test: build it well, list it well, learn from buyers, and improve. if it sells steadily, expand with related templates in the same niche. if it does not, the feedback tells you whether to fix the template, the listing, or the niche itself.

## frequently asked questions

### what templates sell best online?
templates that solve a repeated, specific task tend to sell best: budgets, planners, resumes, content calendars, invoices, and social media packs for a clear audience. a template for a narrow buyer with a clear task usually outsells a generic template aimed at everyone.

### where can i sell templates?
marketplaces such as etsy suit discovery by buyers who search there, while gumroad and payhip suit selling to your own audience with a simple checkout. your own website gives you the most control but needs its own traffic. many sellers start on one marketplace and add their own site later.

### do i need professional design skills to sell templates?
you need clean, usable design, not professional credentials. a template with clear layout, readable type, consistent spacing, and a working structure will outsell a flashy template that confuses buyers. study top listings in your niche to learn the standard, then practise until your work meets it.

### how do i protect my templates from being resold?
use a clear licence, add a credit line inside the file, watermark preview images, and keep your source files and dates. you cannot prevent all sharing, but a clear licence and marketplace reporting handle most cases. focus most of your energy on making the next good template, not on policing the first one.

### should i sell one template or a pack?
start with one strong template to learn the process, then bundle related templates into a pack once you know what buyers want. packs usually earn more per sale and give buyers better value, but a pack of weak templates will not outsell one strong template.

## your next step

your next step is to pick one task your buyers repeat and build the simplest template that completes it well. test it as a stranger, photograph its inside pages for the listing, and publish it on one marketplace with a clear licence and support promise. then watch what buyers ask for, because their questions are your brief for the second template.

for the wider journey, read [how to create your first digital product in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-create-your-first-digital-product) if you have not yet validated an idea, and read [how to price digital products in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-price-digital-products) before you set a final price. for related product types, see [how to create and sell an online course in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-create-and-sell-an-online-course) and [how to sell ebooks and guides online in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-sell-ebooks-online). if you want to compare template selling with other ways of earning from digital skills, read the guide to selling ai art online (/ai-earning/how-to-sell-ai-art-online) and [how to start an online business as a beginner in 2026](/online-business/how-to-start-online-business-beginner).

title: How to Create Your First Digital Product in 2026
excerpt: Learn how to create your first digital product in 2026: pick a problem, validate it fast, build a simple version, and launch it to your first buyers.
coverAlt: A first digital product taking shape on a creator's desk, with a notebook, laptop, and simple product draft
haystack:
how to create your first digital product in 2026 learn how to create your first digital product in 2026: pick a problem, validate it fast, build a simple version, and launch it to your first buyers. digital-products first product beginners digital products a digital product is a file, a template, a guide, or a lesson that a buyer can download or access online. you build it once, and you can sell it many times without restocking a shelf or shipping a parcel. that is why so many beginners start here. the work is real, though. a product nobody wants will not sell just because it is digital, and a good product still needs buyers to find it.

this guide walks you through your first product only: choosing a problem, checking demand, building a small finished version, and selling it to your first buyers. it stays in that lane on purpose. deeper guides on this site cover each product type in full, and the pricing guide covers how to set a price properly. start here, finish one product, and learn from real buyers before you build a second one.

## what counts as a digital product

a digital product solves one problem in a form a buyer can use right away. common first products include a spreadsheet template, a set of social media templates, a short ebook, a checklist bundle, a notion template, a set of presets, or a short video lesson. what they share is a clear promise: buy this, and you get a specific result faster or easier than doing it yourself.

a product is not a vague idea. "productivity" is not a product. "a weekly planner that helps freelance writers track pitches, deadlines, and invoices" is a product. the narrower the promise, the easier it is to describe, price, and sell. beginners often try to serve everyone and end up convincing no one. pick one person with one problem, and build for that person.

## pick a problem worth solving

start with problems, not products. write down ten problems people around you complain about, or questions you keep answering in comments, chats, or at work. good signs: people already pay for a partial solution, people ask the same question repeatedly, or people waste visible time on a task your product could shorten.

then narrow each problem with three questions. who exactly has this problem? what do they currently do instead? what would a solved version look like in one sentence? if you cannot answer all three, the idea is still too vague. for example: "new etsy sellers (who) spend hours guessing at listing titles (current workaround) and want a title worksheet with proven structures (solved version)." that is a product idea. "help people sell online" is not.

avoid problems you cannot verify. if you have never experienced the problem and never talked to anyone who has, you are guessing. talk to five people who have the problem before you build anything. ask what they tried, what frustrated them, and what they would pay to fix. their words will also become your sales page copy later, because you will describe the problem the way buyers describe it.

## validate before you build

validation means checking that strangers, not just supportive friends, want the product. it is the step most beginners skip, and skipping it is the most common reason a first product fails. validation does not need an audience or a budget. it needs a small test and an honest reading of the result.

one simple method is the pre-sell test. write a one page description of the product: who it is for, what it includes, what result it promises, and the price. share it where your target buyers already gather, such as a relevant forum, community, or social group, and invite people to join a waitlist or pre-order. if ten or more strangers sign up or ask questions, you have a signal worth building on. if nobody responds after sharing it in two or three genuinely relevant places, treat that as useful information, not a personal failure. change the problem, the audience, or the promise, and test again.

![a beginner checking validation results for a first digital product idea](/covers/digital-product-validation.jpg)

another method is the search test. search for your product idea and look at what already sells. existing competition is good news, not bad news: it proves buyers exist. read reviews of competing products and note what buyers praise and complain about. complaints are your product brief. if every review of budget spreadsheets says "too complicated for beginners," a simple beginner version is your opening. if no competing product exists at all, be cautious. it may mean there is no demand, or that buyers solve the problem another way.

## choose your first product type

pick the simplest format that delivers the result. a template suits a repeatable task. a short guide suits a process a buyer must understand. a short course suits a skill that needs demonstration. a spreadsheet suits tracking or calculation. do not pick video just because video feels premium; video takes far longer to record, edit, and update, and a buyer who wants a quick template will not thank you for a two hour course.

| product type | best when the buyer needs | typical first effort | starter price range only |
|---|---|---|---|
| template or worksheet | to do a task faster | low: hours to days | low single figures to low double figures |
| short ebook or guide | to understand a process | medium: days to weeks | low single figures to low double figures |
| spreadsheet or tracker | to track or calculate | low to medium | low single figures to low double figures |
| short video course | to learn a demonstrated skill | high: weeks | low double figures and up |
| preset, asset, or resource pack | ready made parts to use | low to medium | low single figures to low double figures |

the starter ranges above are only a rough starting point for a first product. full pricing method, including fees, tiers, and bundles, belongs in the pricing guide linked below, and you should read it before you set a final price. for your first product, a lower price is often wiser: it lowers the barrier for a buyer who does not know you yet, and it gets you feedback and testimonials faster.

## build a small, finished version

set a build deadline of two to four weeks and a clear finish line: a file a buyer can download, a sales page, and a way to take payment. work backwards from that finish line. list every piece the product needs, cut anything that is nice to have, and build the core first. test it yourself as a buyer would: download it, open it on a phone and a computer, and follow its instructions without your own inside knowledge. fix anything confusing before launch.

## set up a simple sales page

you do not need a full website to sell a first product, though this site's online business guides cover building one when you are ready. a sales page on a platform such as gumroad, payhip, or etsy can handle payment, delivery, and basic tax handling. compare platforms on the features you need: ease of setup, checkout experience, fees, and whether buyers can find you through the platform itself. fees change, so check each platform's live fee page before you commit, and include those fees in your price calculation rather than discovering them after your first sale.

your sales page needs six elements: a clear title that names the result, a short description of who it is for, a list of exactly what is included, a preview (a screenshot, a sample page, or a short video), the price, and a refund policy. show the product, not just describe it. a buyer who can see a template page or read a sample chapter trusts the product far more than a buyer who only reads promises. if you have no testimonials yet, say nothing rather than inventing any. early buyers and honest reviews will fill that gap.

## launch to your first buyers

a launch is simply telling the right people, in the right places, that the product exists and is ready to buy. start with the people who showed interest during validation: your waitlist, the communities where you tested the idea, and anyone who asked for updates. tell them first, and give them a reason to act now, such as a launch price that rises after a set date. early buyers give you feedback, reviews, and proof that the product works for real users.

![a simple launch checklist for a first digital product](/covers/digital-product-launch.jpg)

then expand one channel at a time. one channel done well beats five channels done badly. if your buyers gather on one platform, post genuinely useful content there and link the product where it helps, rather than posting the same sales message everywhere. answer questions, share a sample, and let the product's usefulness do the persuading. keep a simple record of where each sale came from, so you know which channel deserves more effort next time.

## risks, limits, and honest expectations

digital products have real limits. income is not automatic and not passive at first: you still need to find buyers, answer questions, and update the product. sales can be slow for weeks, especially without an audience. refunds happen, platforms change rules and fees, and products can become outdated. keep costs low, do not borrow money to build a first product, and do not quit a stable income on the hope of first product sales.

results vary with your niche, your audience, your price, your product quality, and how consistently you promote it. two people can build similar products and get very different results because their audiences and timing differ. treat income claims from sellers with caution, especially claims without evidence. your own first product is an experiment with a low cost and a useful lesson, whatever the sales number.

legal and tax basics also matter. you are responsible for the tax and legal rules that apply to you, and those rules vary by country. selling platforms handle some tax collection, but not necessarily all of it. if your product gives advice in a regulated area such as finance, health, or law, be careful: present general information, explain your limits, and do not present yourself as a licensed professional unless you are one. when in doubt, keep the product in an area you genuinely know, and check local rules before you scale.

## frequently asked questions

### what is the easiest first digital product to create?
the easiest first product is usually a template, worksheet, or checklist. it needs no recording, no long writing, and a buyer can judge its value from a preview. pick a task your target buyer repeats, and make it faster or simpler.

### how long does a first digital product take to build?
a simple template or checklist can take a weekend. a short guide usually takes one to three weeks. a short video course usually takes three to six weeks including recording and editing. set a deadline before you start, and cut scope rather than extending the deadline indefinitely.

### do i need an audience before i sell a digital product?
no, but you need a way to reach buyers. without an audience, your reach comes from search, marketplaces, communities, and useful content posted where buyers gather. validation without an audience is possible, as described above, but expect slower early sales and plan to build an audience alongside the product.

### how much should i charge for my first digital product?
start low enough that a stranger can say yes without much thought, and high enough that the sale feels worthwhile after fees. the starter ranges in the table above are a rough guide only. read the full pricing guide before you set a final price, and check each platform's live fee page.

### what if nobody buys my first product?
treat it as data. ask the people who saw it why they did not buy, check whether the problem or the price was wrong, and check whether you reached the right buyers at all. many first products fail on reach or problem choice, not on quality. fix one variable, relaunch, or move to a better validated idea.

## your next step

your next step is a one week validation test. write down ten problems, pick the strongest one, and test it with a one page description shared where your buyers gather. if strangers respond, build the smallest finished version and launch it. if they do not, change one variable and test again. one finished product and ten honest sales will teach you more about selling digital products than months of planning.

to go deeper, read the type specific guides next: [how to sell templates online in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-sell-templates-online), [how to create and sell an online course in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-create-and-sell-an-online-course), and [how to sell ebooks and guides online in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-sell-ebooks-online). before you set your price, read [how to price digital products in 2026](/digital-products/how-to-price-digital-products). if you are still deciding whether a digital product fits your wider plan, read [how to start an online business as a beginner in 2026](/online-business/how-to-start-online-business-beginner) and [online business models explained: which one fits you in 2026](/online-business/online-business-models-explained).

title: How to Get Your First Customers for a New Online Business in 2026
excerpt: Win your first ten customers with conversations before ads: clear offers, short outreach templates, honest reviews, referrals, and a simple tracker.
coverAlt: A new shop owner greeting a first customer at a small online store setup with a laptop and parcels
haystack:
how to get your first customers for a new online business in 2026 win your first ten customers with conversations before ads: clear offers, short outreach templates, honest reviews, referrals, and a simple tracker. online-business first-customers marketing-for-beginners online business 
a new online business with no customers faces a strange problem: buyers want proof before they buy, but proof comes from buyers. the way out is smaller than most guides suggest. you do not need an audience, a viral post, or an advertising budget to get your first customers. you need a clear offer, a list of likely buyers, and a series of helpful conversations that lead, naturally, to a sale. this guide is built around the first ten customers, because ten paying customers teach you more about pricing, delivery, and language than a thousand views ever will. the first ten principle is simple: conversations before ads. paid advertising amplifies an offer that already works; it rarely fixes an offer nobody understands or trusts.



## before you chase customers: is your offer clear in one sentence?

before any outreach, test your offer with one sentence: who it helps, what outcome it delivers, and what the next step is. for example: "i write four menu graphics a month for small food businesses, delivered every monday, for one monthly price, starting with a paid trial week." a stranger should understand the buyer, the outcome, and the action without asking a follow up question. if your sentence needs a paragraph of explanation, the offer is still too broad, and outreach will produce confusion instead of sales. run an offer clarity checklist before you contact anyone. can a stranger name the buyer from your sentence? can they name the outcome? can they see what is included and what is not? can they see the price or the next step?



## the first ten principle: conversations before ads

your first ten customers will almost certainly come from conversations, not from campaigns. that means your daily work in the early stage is not designing posts or studying analytics, but talking to likely buyers, answering their questions, and inviting a clear next step. set a simple activity goal, such as ten useful conversations a week, and judge the week by that number plus replies, not by followers or views. a week with ten conversations and two replies teaches you something. a week with no conversations teaches you nothing, however busy it felt. conversations also build the language your business will use later. buyers will describe their problem in their own words, ask questions you had not considered, and object in ways that reveal price, trust, or timing concerns.



## path a: services, freelance marketplaces and direct outreach

for services, the fastest first customer route is usually a combination of marketplaces and direct outreach. on a freelance marketplace, your profile is your shop window: one clear service, a few strong examples, a realistic starting price, and a description written in the buyer's language. apply only to jobs that fit your package closely, and write proposals that refer to the buyer's actual problem, not a generic pitch. a short proposal that shows you understood the job beats a long proposal that lists every skill you own. for a fuller freelance starting path, see [how to find freelance clients](/freelancing/how-to-find-freelance-clients) and [how to create a freelance portfolio](/freelancing/how-to-create-a-freelance-portfolio). direct outreach complements marketplaces, because it reaches buyers who have not posted a job. list twenty to fifty likely buyers, research each one briefly, and send a short personal message (templates are below).



## path b: digital products, marketplaces and searchable content

digital products rarely sell on outreach alone, because buyers usually search for a solution when they need it. your first customers therefore come from being findable where buyers search. list your product on a marketplace that already has traffic for your category, with a clear title, an honest description, a preview, and a price that covers fees. use the words buyers actually type when they search, not clever wording that only you understand. a single product, well listed, beats ten thin listings that confuse search and split reviews. searchable content is the second route: short articles, videos, or posts that answer the exact question your product solves, with a clear link to the product at the end.



## path c: physical products, early reviewers, communities, and micro creators

physical products need trust before purchase, because buyers cannot touch the product and worry about quality, delivery, and returns. early reviewers solve part of that problem, if handled honestly. offer a small number of early buyers a fair introductory price or a sample in exchange for an honest review, with no condition that the review must be positive. never buy fake reviews, never write your own reviews, and never offer payment for positive ratings, because that destroys trust and can breach platform rules. a handful of honest reviews, including a critical one you respond to well, is more persuasive than a wall of identical praise. communities are the second route for physical products: groups where buyers discuss the hobby, problem, or lifestyle your product serves.



## outreach that gets replies: three short templates (and what not to send)

good outreach is short, personal, and specific. it shows you understood the buyer, offers one clear outcome, and asks for one simple reply. bad outreach is long, generic, and self focused: a list of your skills, a vague offer, and pressure to reply. never send the same message to fifty people with only the name changed and expect replies, because buyers can tell. never claim a connection you do not have, never invent a result, and never follow up aggressively. one polite follow up is enough.

![a person writing a short friendly message on a laptop in a cafe](/covers/outreach-templates.jpg)

template 1, for services: "hello [name], i noticed [specific detail about their business or post]. i help [buyer type] with [outcome], usually through [one package].



## turn buyers into proof: honest reviews and testimonials, done properly

after a sale, proof is the next asset to build, and it must be honest to be useful. ask for a review at the right moment: after delivery, once the buyer has had a chance to use the product or see the result, and when satisfaction is fresh. make it easy: send a direct link, suggest two or three prompts, such as what problem they had, what changed, and what they would tell a friend, and thank them whatever they write. use their exact words where permission is given, and never edit a testimonial to change its meaning. if a review is critical, respond calmly, fix what you can, and treat the exchange as public evidence of good service. testimonials need the same care.



## referrals without awkwardness, and your first email list

referrals feel awkward when asked too early, too vaguely, or with pressure. they feel natural when asked after a good delivery, with a specific request. the right moment is after a buyer is happy: they have thanked you, used the product, or told you the result helped. at that point, a simple ask works: "i am glad that helped. if you know one person with the same problem, would you be happy to pass my name on, or introduce us?" that ask is specific (one person), low pressure (would you be happy to), and tied to a real result. make referrals easy to give: provide a short description the buyer can forward, a link to your offer, and a clear next step for the new person.



## track it simply: reach, replies, interest, sales, and source

![a simple tracking spreadsheet and notebook on a desk](/covers/customer-tracker.jpg)

a simple tracker turns outreach from guesswork into a system. record five numbers each week, by source: reach (how many likely buyers saw your offer or message), replies (how many responded), interest (how many asked about price, timing, or details), sales (how many paid), and source (marketplace, community, outreach, content, referral, or email). a spreadsheet with one row per week and one column per number is enough. the pattern between the numbers tells you where to work next, and it prevents the common mistake of changing everything at once. use the tracker to set realistic activity goals. if your reply rate is low, improve your message or your buyer list, not your website. if replies are high but interest is low, improve offer clarity.



## if nobody responds: diagnose the weak link before quitting

a dry spell is painful, but it is also information, if you diagnose it in order. work through four possible weak links, one at a time. first, wrong people: are you contacting buyers who actually have the problem and can pay, or a broad audience that merely finds the topic interesting? second, unclear offer: can a stranger name the buyer, outcome, and next step from your message in seconds? third, weak trust: do you have any proof, examples, reviews, or a clear presence that a stranger can check, or are you asking for payment on the strength of a new profile alone? fourth, too little traffic: have you actually contacted enough of the right people, or have you sent ten messages and concluded the market is dead? test each link with a small change and watch the tracker.



## after ten customers, and risks

after ten paying customers, your job shifts from finding any buyer to building a repeatable system. systematise what already works: a standard package, a delivery checklist, a welcome message, a review request, and a referral ask after each good delivery. write down the steps you repeat, so delivery stays consistent when volume grows. improve your best channel first: if outreach brings customers, refine your list and templates; if a marketplace brings them, improve listings and reviews; if content brings them, publish the next helpful piece on the same topic. do not add three new channels at ten customers. depth in one proven channel beats breadth across unproven ones.



## faqs

### how do i get my first customer with no audience?
start with conversations where buyers already gather: a marketplace, a community, or direct outreach to likely buyers. offer one clear package or product, show examples or samples, and ask for a specific next step, such as a trial, a booking, or a purchase. an audience helps later, but your first customers usually come from personal outreach and helpful answers, not from a large following.

### should i run ads to get my first customers?
usually not. ads amplify an offer that already sells, but they rarely fix unclear offers, weak trust, or a wrong audience, and they spend money before you know your numbers. get your first customers through free conversations, marketplaces, and communities first, learn what converts, and consider a small, strictly limited ad test only after the offer sells reliably without ads.

### how do i ask for referrals?
ask after a good delivery, when the buyer is happy, and keep it specific and low pressure: ask whether they know one person with the same problem and whether they would be happy to pass your name on. provide a short description and a link they can forward. do not ask vaguely, do not pressure, and do not offer misleading incentives. one warm referral often converts better than many cold messages.

### how many customers do i need before paid ads make sense?
there is no fixed number, but ten paying customers through free routes is a sensible minimum, because by then you know your offer, price, conversion pattern, and value per sale after fees. with those numbers, you can judge whether an ad test is affordable. if you do not yet know what a sale is worth or how many enquiries become sales, ads are still a guess, not a test.

### what is the cheapest way to get customers?
the cheapest routes are usually marketplace search, helpful answers in communities, direct outreach, and referrals from happy buyers, because they cost time rather than money. the cheapest route for you depends on your business type: services suit outreach and marketplaces, digital products suit marketplaces and searchable content, and physical products suit communities, early reviewers, and micro creators. track each route and spend more time on the one that actually brings sales.



## conclusion: your next step

your first customers will not arrive because your business exists. they will arrive because a clear offer reached the right people, through helpful conversations, and earned their trust one sale at a time. check your offer in one sentence, choose the path that fits your business type, use short honest outreach, turn each buyer into proof with permission, ask for referrals after good deliveries, start a tiny email list, and track reach, replies, interest, sales, and source every week. when silence comes, diagnose the weak link before quitting, and change one thing at a time. your next step is to list twenty likely buyers today, write your one sentence offer, and send the first three outreach messages using the template that fits your type. do not wait for an audience, a perfect website, or an advertising budget. ten conversations this week, followed by a review of what happened, will teach you more than another month of preparation, and those conversations are where your first ten customers are waiting to be found.
