10 common freelancing mistakes to avoid ten common freelancing mistakes that cost beginners money and clients, from underpricing and missing contracts to burnout, and how to fix each one. freelancing mistakes beginners freelancing most freelancing mistakes are not dramatic. they are small decisions that seem harmless at the time: a low rate to win a client, a handshake instead of a contract, one more project when the calendar is already full. months later they show up as an empty bank account, a client dispute, or burnout. this guide covers the ten mistakes that catch beginners most often, what each one costs, and how to fix it.

## 1. underpricing your work

this is the most common freelancing mistake, and it starts with good intentions. you charge less because you are afraid of losing the client, or because you are new and feel you should prove yourself first.

the cost is real. charge $10 below your target rate across 20 billable hours a week and you lose $200 a week, or more than $10,000 a year. low rates also attract the hardest clients: people who haggle, demand extra work, and leave for someone cheaper.

**how to fix it:** calculate your minimum rate from your real costs instead of copying your old salary. our guide to [setting freelance rates](/freelancing/how-to-set-freelance-rates) shows the full formula. if you start with an introductory rate, write down the date you will raise it, and tell the client it is an introductory price.

## 2. working without a contract

starting work on a verbal agreement feels friendly and fast. it also leaves you with nothing to point to when the scope changes, the payment is late, or the client disappears.

a contract does not need to be long or legalistic. a simple written agreement should cover:

- project scope and deliverables
- timeline and deadlines
- payment amount and schedule
- revision limits
- ownership and usage rights
- cancellation terms

use it for every project, including small ones and including work for friends. platforms like upwork include contracts and milestone payments automatically, which is one reason many beginners start there.

## 3. not asking for payment upfront

waiting until the end of a project to get paid means you carry all the risk. if the client goes quiet, you have done the work and have nothing to show for it.

**how to fix it:** ask for a deposit of 30 to 50 percent before you start, or break larger projects into milestones with payment due at each step. for small jobs, payment in full before starting is reasonable. a client who refuses any upfront payment is telling you something about how they treat freelancers.

dolinks' guide [common freelancing mistakes to avoid](https://dolinks.net/common-freelancing-mistakes/) tells the same story through a beginner's first year: a low rate, a late payment, and no contract, each one fixable with a simple system.

## 4. saying yes to every project

when work is scarce, every enquiry feels like an opportunity. saying yes to all of them fills your calendar with rushed work, low budgets, and clients who do not respect your time. your best clients, the ones who pay on time and value your work, get squeezed out by the worst ones.

**how to fix it:** decide in advance what a good project looks like: the right service, a realistic budget, a clear brief, and a client you can communicate with. turn down the rest politely. a short "i am fully booked this month, but i can start in three weeks" protects your time and your reputation.

## 5. poor communication

most freelancer-client conflicts start with unclear expectations, not bad work. the client expected daily updates and got silence. you expected feedback in two days and waited a week. nobody said anything until it became a problem.

**how to fix it:** agree on communication at the start of every project: how often you will update them, which channel to use, how fast you reply, and what happens if either side is delayed. send a short progress update even when there is nothing dramatic to report. clients who hear from you regularly trust you more and refer you more.

![close-up of hands signing a paper contract with a pen, a laptop and a coffee cup softly out of focus behind](/covers/freelance-contract.jpg)

## 6. ignoring taxes and admin

spending every payment as it arrives feels fine until the tax bill comes. freelancers pay their own taxes, and in many countries they pay them in instalments during the year, not once at the end. a freelancer who saves nothing for tax can owe months of income at once.

**how to fix it:** set aside a portion of every payment in a separate account, from the first invoice. the right portion depends on where you live and how much you earn, so check your local tax rules early or ask an accountant for a one-hour consultation. keep every invoice and receipt in one place. ten minutes of admin per project is enough if you do it as you go.

## 7. not tracking time or setting boundaries

without office structure, work expands to fill every hour. you answer messages at midnight, take on rush jobs on weekends, and skip breaks because there is always one more email. the result is burnout, and burned-out freelancers deliver worse work, not more of it.

**how to fix it:** track your hours for a month, including admin and communication, so you know where your time actually goes. set working hours and tell clients what they are. block time for rest the same way you block time for client work. if you are fully booked, raise your rates instead of adding more hours. a waiting list is a pricing signal, not a problem.

## 8. offering every service to every client

trying to be a jack-of-all-trades dilutes your expertise and makes you harder to hire. a client looking for a landing page will choose the freelancer who builds landing pages over the one who also does logos, videos, bookkeeping, and social media.

**how to fix it:** pick one main service and one type of client, and let your portfolio and profiles reflect that choice. you can add a second service later, once the first one brings steady work. specialists are easier to find, easier to trust, and easier to pay well.

## 9. neglecting your portfolio

many freelancers build a portfolio once and never touch it again. months later it shows old work, broken links, and services they no longer offer, while their best recent projects are nowhere to be found.

**how to fix it:** update your portfolio after every project you are proud of, while the details are fresh. remove the weakest piece each time you add a stronger one. our guide to [creating a freelance portfolio](/freelancing/how-to-create-a-freelance-portfolio) explains what to include, how many projects to show, and how to write short case studies.

## 10. working for exposure or breaking platform rules

two related mistakes catch beginners. the first is accepting unpaid work in exchange for "exposure" or a promise of future paid work. exposure does not pay rent, and clients who ask for free work rarely become paying clients. a small paid trial is a fair alternative.

the second is breaking the rules of the platform you work on: moving chats or payments off a marketplace to avoid fees, or asking a client to pay outside the platform's protection. platforms suspend accounts for this, and losing your profile means losing your reviews, your history, and your income channel. read the rules of any platform you use, and keep payments inside it until you have a direct relationship and a contract of your own.

![a freelancer closing a laptop and walking outdoors with a bag in bright daylight, relaxed after work](/covers/freelance-work-balance.jpg)

## a pre-flight checklist for every project

run through this list before you start any new project. it takes two minutes and prevents most of the mistakes above.

| check | done? |
|---|---|
| scope, deliverables, and deadlines are written down | |
| payment terms and deposit are agreed | |
| revision limits are stated | |
| your rate covers your costs (not just your old wage) | |
| the project fits your niche and your calendar | |
| you have a sample or proof for this type of work | |
| tax portion of the payment is set aside | |
| the client is reachable and communicates clearly | |

## how to recover if you have already made these mistakes

most freelancing mistakes are fixable, and most freelancers make them. raise your rates for new clients first, then give existing clients notice. send a short written agreement for future work, even to clients you already work with. block out your calendar for the coming month and say no to the next project that does not fit. update your profile headline to reflect a clear niche. then message two past clients you enjoyed working with: a friendly check-in often turns into repeat work or a referral.

plustechnology's short guide [5 freelancing mistakes beginners should avoid](https://plustechnology.co/top-5-freelancing-mistakes-to-avoid-as-a-beginner/) makes the same point: undercharging, skipping contracts, poor time management, no niche, and neglecting clients are the five that matter most, and each one has a simple fix.

## frequently asked questions

### what is the most common freelancing mistake?

underpricing. charging too little leads to burnout, attracts clients who value price over quality, and leaves no room to grow. calculate your rate from your real costs and raise it as you gain experience.

### do freelancers really need contracts?

yes. a simple agreement covering scope, payment terms, and deadlines prevents most disputes. even a one-page document is enough, and marketplace platforms include contracts automatically.

### how do i avoid late payments as a freelancer?

use clear contracts with payment terms, ask for a deposit or milestone payments, and use platforms that hold client payments until work is approved. follow up politely but promptly when a payment is overdue.

### should a beginner freelancer choose a niche?

yes. a clear niche makes you easier to find, easier to trust, and easier to pay well. you can widen it later once you have steady work.

### how do i recover from freelancing mistakes?

fix one thing at a time. raise rates for new clients, put future work in writing, protect your calendar, and reconnect with past clients. most mistakes are recoverable within a month or two of steady, deliberate changes.

## conclusion

the ten mistakes in this guide share one root cause: treating freelancing as a gig instead of a business. price your work from real costs, put agreements in writing, ask for payment upfront, protect your time, and keep your portfolio current. do those things and most of the rest takes care of itself. if you are at the very beginning, start with our guide to [starting freelancing](/freelancing/how-to-start-freelancing), then work through [finding clients](/freelancing/how-to-find-freelance-clients) and [setting your rates](/freelancing/how-to-set-freelance-rates) with this checklist beside you. you can browse all of our [freelancing guides](/freelancing) for the full collection.

title: How to Set Freelance Rates: A Practical Guide
excerpt: A practical guide to setting freelance rates: calculate your minimum rate from real costs, check market rates, choose a pricing model, and raise your rates.
coverAlt: A calculator, a notebook with handwritten notes, and a laptop on a wooden desk
haystack:
how to set freelance rates: a practical guide a practical guide to setting freelance rates: calculate your minimum rate from real costs, check market rates, choose a pricing model, and raise your rates. freelancing pricing rates freelancing setting freelance rates is the part most beginners get wrong, usually by guessing. the most common mistake is copying your old hourly wage, or charging whatever the client suggests. both leave you underpaid, because a freelance rate has to cover things an employer used to pay for: taxes, insurance, retirement, holidays, and all the hours you cannot bill. this guide shows you how to calculate a rate that pays your bills, check it against the market, choose a pricing model, and raise it with confidence.

## why your old salary is the wrong starting point

an employee earning $50,000 a year costs their employer much more than $50,000. the employer also pays payroll taxes, health insurance, retirement contributions, paid holidays, equipment, and office costs. as a freelancer, you pay all of that yourself, out of your rate.

that is why freelance rates need to be much higher than the equivalent hourly wage. if your old job paid $25 an hour, a freelance rate of $25 an hour means a pay cut, not a match. the exact multiple depends on your costs and your country, but a rate roughly two to three times the equivalent employee wage is common. the formula below shows you how to work out your own number instead of guessing.

## step 1: add up your real costs

start with what you need to live on, then add the costs of running your business. use your own currency and your own numbers. the figures in the table are examples in us dollars to show the method.

| cost | what to include | example (annual) |
|---|---|---|
| target take-home pay | what you want to earn after tax | $60,000 |
| income tax and self-employment tax | set aside a share of every payment; rates depend on your country | $12,000 |
| health insurance | premiums for you, and family if relevant | $6,000 |
| retirement savings | what you would have saved as an employee, plus any employer match you lose | $6,000 |
| business expenses | software, equipment, internet, phone, accounting, marketing | $4,000 |
| time off | holidays and sick days you now pay for yourself | $4,000 |
| **total revenue needed** | | **$92,000** |

if you are outside the united states, replace the tax line with your own country's rules. in the us, self-employed workers pay a self-employment tax of about 15.3 percent on most net earnings, on top of income tax. in other countries the structure is different, so check your local tax authority or an accountant before you set your rate.

## step 2: work out your billable hours

you will not bill 40 hours a week. between finding clients, writing proposals, invoicing, admin, and learning, most freelancers bill 20 to 30 hours a week. plan for it honestly.

a realistic estimate:

- 52 weeks minus 4 weeks of holiday and sick days: 48 working weeks.
- 25 billable hours a week (the rest is admin, sales, and learning).
- 48 times 25: **1,200 billable hours a year.**

if you assume 40 billable hours a week, your rate will look comfortable on paper and leave you short in real life. track your hours for a month before you commit to a number; it is the fastest way to learn your real billable ratio.

![a notebook page with a simple handwritten calculation and a pen, a calculator beside it](/covers/freelance-rate-formula.jpg)

## step 3: calculate your minimum rate

divide the revenue you need by your billable hours:

**$92,000 divided by 1,200 hours = about $77 an hour**

that is your floor: the lowest rate that meets your goals. it is not your target. your target should sit above it, because projects run over, clients pay late, and some months are slow. many freelancers add a margin of 20 to 30 percent above their floor as a buffer, and treat the floor as the number they never go below.

try the same calculation with your own numbers before you quote your next project. it takes ten minutes and it changes how you negotiate.

## step 4: check market rates

your minimum rate tells you what you need. market research tells you what clients will pay. if your floor is far above the market, you need to cut costs, bill more hours, specialise in a higher-paying niche, or move to project pricing. if your floor is far below the market, you are leaving money on the table.

where to find real data:

- **salary data for your skill.** search job sites for full-time roles in your field. divide the annual salary by about 2,000 hours for an hourly baseline, then add 30 to 50 percent, because freelancers do not get benefits. the us bureau of labor statistics [occupational outlook handbook](https://www.bls.gov/) lists median pay by occupation and is a useful anchor.
- **rate surveys in your field.** professional associations and industry publications often publish annual rate surveys.
- **other freelancers.** ask peers in communities and forums what they charge for similar work. people share ranges more often than you expect.
- **your own results.** track what you win and lose. if you win every proposal, your rates are probably too low.

ownworkhq's guide [how to set freelance rates: 7 steps + free example](https://ownworkhq.com/how-to-set-freelance-rates/) works through the same formula with a full example, including a table that shows how fewer billable hours push the required rate up.

## step 5: choose a pricing model

| model | how it works | best for | watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| hourly | you bill tracked time | unclear scope, ongoing support | punishes efficiency; clients watch the clock |
| project (fixed fee) | one price for defined deliverables | clear scope: websites, logos, articles | scope creep without a good contract |
| day rate | fixed price per day | on-site work, workshops | define what a day includes |
| retainer | monthly fee for ongoing work | long-term clients | define hours or deliverables included |
| value-based | price based on the outcome's worth to the client | experienced freelancers with measurable impact | requires understanding the client's business |

for your first projects, hourly or project pricing is simplest. project pricing rewards efficiency and is easier for clients to budget, as long as the scope is written down. a useful hybrid for beginners is a fixed project price with an hourly rate for extra work: "this project is $1,500 for the defined scope. additional work beyond the scope is billed at $80 an hour."

spunk's guide [how to set your freelance rates in 2026](https://spunk.work/blog/how-to-set-freelance-rates-2026) compares the same models and includes a rate table by skill, which is useful for a rough market check.

## how to quote a project price

quoting by project is a skill. follow these steps:

1. break the project into tasks and estimate hours for each.
2. multiply by your hourly rate.
3. add a buffer of 15 to 25 percent for communication, revisions, and surprises.
4. round to a clean number and present it as a fixed fee with a clear scope.

| task | hours | at $77 an hour |
|---|---|---|
| discovery call and brief | 2 | $154 |
| draft 5 website pages | 12 | $924 |
| two revision rounds | 4 | $308 |
| project management and email | 2 | $154 |
| subtotal | 20 | $1,540 |
| buffer (20 percent) | | $308 |
| **quoted project fee** | | **$1,850** |

put the scope and the number of revision rounds in your contract, so extra work is billed separately instead of given away.

![a laptop screen showing three simple pricing tier cards, a notebook and a coffee cup on the desk](/covers/freelance-pricing-models.jpg)

## what to do when a client says your rate is too high

this is not always a rejection. it is often the start of a negotiation. do not discount your rate on the spot. instead:

- ask what range they had in mind. that tells you whether the gap is small or impossible.
- reduce the scope instead of the price. "i can do the first three pages within that budget. the full five pages would be $1,850."
- explain what is included: revisions, research, communication, and delivery. clients compare prices, but they buy the whole package.
- say your rate once, then stop talking. silence is not rudeness; it gives the client room to answer.

if nobody ever pushes back on your rates, you are probably undercharging. a healthy close rate is roughly one in three proposals, not ten in ten.

## when and how to raise your rates

review your rates at least once a year, and raise them when you are fully booked, when you add a skill, or when your costs rise. apply the new rate to new clients first. for existing clients, give 30 to 60 days of notice and keep the message short:

"starting 1 march, my rate for new projects will be $85 an hour. anything we agree before then stays at the current rate. thank you for working with me, and i look forward to our next project."

you can also build a simple rate card: a one-page list of your standard prices for common services. it speeds up quoting, keeps you consistent, and helps clients understand what they are buying. review it every six months. if you are consistently booked, raise the prices on the card first.

## common pricing mistakes

- using your old hourly wage as your freelance rate.
- assuming 40 billable hours a week.
- forgetting taxes, insurance, and retirement.
- discounting heavily to win a first client and getting stuck at that rate.
- not charging for revisions, rush work, or scope changes.
- quoting on the spot instead of taking a day to scope the work properly.
- charging the same rate for every client, regardless of urgency or complexity.
- never revisiting the numbers as costs and skills change.

if you are just starting out, read our guide to [starting freelancing](/freelancing/how-to-start-freelancing) for the full sequence, and our guide to [common freelancing mistakes](/freelancing/common-freelancing-mistakes) for the pricing errors that cost beginners the most.

## frequently asked questions

### how do i calculate my freelance hourly rate?

add your target income, business expenses, insurance, retirement savings, and taxes, then divide by your realistic billable hours per year. compare the result with market rates and adjust.

### how many billable hours do freelancers work?

most bill 1,000 to 1,300 hours a year, or roughly 20 to 30 hours a week across 46 to 48 working weeks. the rest goes to admin, marketing, and learning.

### should freelancers charge hourly or per project?

hourly works for unclear or ongoing work. project pricing rewards efficiency and is easier for clients to budget, as long as the scope is clearly defined in a contract. many beginners start hourly and move to project pricing as they gain experience.

### how much higher should a freelance rate be than a salary?

often around two to three times the equivalent hourly wage, because you cover taxes, benefits, expenses, and unbillable time. the exact multiple depends on your costs and billable hours, so run the formula with your own numbers.

### how often should i raise my freelance rates?

review them at least once a year. raise rates for new clients first and give existing clients notice before changing theirs. if you are fully booked, that is the clearest sign your rates are too low.

## conclusion

a freelance rate is a calculation, not a guess. add up your real costs, divide by the hours you can actually bill, check the market, and treat the result as your floor. then choose a pricing model that fits the work, quote projects with a buffer, and raise your rates when demand proves you can. run the numbers once, write them down, and quote with confidence. for the next step, make sure your proof is ready with our guide to [creating a freelance portfolio](/freelancing/how-to-create-a-freelance-portfolio), and put your rate to work with our guide to [finding freelance clients](/freelancing/how-to-find-freelance-clients). you can browse all of our [freelancing guides](/freelancing) for the full collection.

title: Create a Freelance Portfolio That Gets You Hired
excerpt: Learn how to create a freelance portfolio that wins clients: what to include, how many projects to show, how to write case studies, and where to build it.
coverAlt: A laptop on a desk displaying a clean portfolio website with large project photos
haystack:
create a freelance portfolio that gets you hired learn how to create a freelance portfolio that wins clients: what to include, how many projects to show, how to write case studies, and where to build it. freelancing portfolio clients freelancing a freelance portfolio is the proof behind your pitch. when a client considers hiring you, the portfolio is where they decide. it is not a gallery of everything you have ever made. it is a short, focused argument: here is the work i do, here is who i do it for, and here is why you can trust me with your project.

## what clients actually look for

clients scan portfolios fast, usually in under a minute. they are looking for four things:

- **relevance.** work that looks like the project they need. a wedding photographer does not care about your product shots.
- **quality.** a few strong pieces beat twenty average ones.
- **results.** what changed because of your work? even a simple result counts: faster page, clearer message, more bookings.
- **ease.** can they contact you in one click? if they have to hunt for your email, they leave.

everything in your portfolio should serve one of those four checks. anything else is decoration.

## how many projects to show

show six to twelve projects if you have them, in the order you want to be hired for. put the work you want more of first, even if it is not your most liked or most recent piece.

if you have fewer than six, show three to five strong ones. a small, sharp portfolio beats a large, uneven one. never pad it with weak work to reach a number. clients judge you by your weakest piece, not your best.

keep older work in an archive page, or remove it. a portfolio that shows your growth is good; a portfolio that shows work you would no longer accept is not.

## what to include when you have no clients yet

this is the question every beginner asks, and the answer is simple: make your own projects and label them honestly as samples.

**for writers:** publish two or three sample articles on real topics. write them to the standard a client would pay for, and publish them where anyone can read them.

**for designers:** redesign a real local business: a menu, a social media post, or a logo. show the original next to your version and explain what you improved.

**for developers:** build a complete small website for an imaginary business and put it online. a live link beats a screenshot.

**for video editors:** cut three short videos from free stock footage. show different styles: one fast-paced, one calm, one with captions.

**for virtual assistants:** build a sample system: a tidy spreadsheet, an inbox workflow, or a notion workspace, and record a two-minute walkthrough.

for every sample, write the same three lines: what the project needed, what you did, and what the result was. if it is a sample, say so clearly. inventing a client is dishonest and easy to discover. if you are starting from zero, our guide to [starting freelancing](/freelancing/how-to-start-freelancing) explains how to pick a service and a niche first.

## how to write a short case study

a case study is a project with a story. it does not need to be long. three short paragraphs are enough:

1. **the problem.** what did the client need? one or two sentences.
2. **what you did.** your approach and the decisions you made. keep it specific: the tools, the structure, the choices.
3. **the result.** what changed? use a number only if it is real and you can explain how it was measured. if you have no number, describe the outcome in plain words: the client launched on time, the page is easier to use, the booking form works.

add a short client quote only if it is genuine and you have permission to use it. two real quotes beat ten anonymous ones.

![a designer's desk with printed project samples, color swatches, and a tablet showing design work](/covers/freelance-portfolio-samples.jpg)

## choosing where to build it

you have three realistic options. pick the one you will actually finish and maintain.

| option | best for | cost | watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| your own website | writers, designers, developers, anyone building a brand | domain and hosting, usually low | takes a day or two to set up well |
| portfolio builders | anyone who wants a page fast without code | often free to start | less control, and your work sits on someone else's platform |
| marketplace profiles | beginners who need clients quickly | free, but the platform takes a fee on work | clients see you next to competitors |

most freelancers end up with two: a simple personal website as the home base, and a marketplace profile where clients search. link them to each other.

if you build your own site, use a clean template and your own domain name if you can. your name plus a short domain is still the most professional portfolio address there is. if you use a builder, check that it lets you use your own domain later, so you are not locked in.

cloudeel's guide [how to build a freelancer portfolio that gets you hired](https://cloudeel.com/blog/freelancer-portfolio-website-guide) makes the same point well: a portfolio should work as a filter that attracts the clients you want and gently turns away the ones you do not.

## what to put on the first screen

the first screen decides whether a client scrolls or leaves. it needs four things:

- **one sentence about who you help.** "brand identity for food and drink startups" beats "designer. dreamer. coffee lover."
- **three of your best projects.** large images, short titles, no clutter.
- **a short list of services with starting prices, if you are comfortable sharing them.** prices filter out clients who cannot afford you and save everyone time.
- **a clear way to contact you.** a button and an email address, visible without scrolling.

skip the skills bar chart ("photoshop 90 percent" tells a client nothing), the "under construction" section, and the blog you will never update. publish what is finished and add the rest later.

## services and prices: should you list them?

listing starting prices is optional, but it helps more than it hurts. a services block that says "website copy, from $450 a page" means every enquiry already knows the range. you lose the people who would have wasted your time, and the rest arrive better prepared.

if your work is always custom-quoted, list the services without prices and add a typical timeline instead, such as "most projects take 2 to 4 weeks". either way, be consistent: if you list prices in one place, keep them current everywhere. our guide to [setting freelance rates](/freelancing/how-to-set-freelance-rates) shows how to calculate a rate that covers your real costs.

## trust signals that work (and fake ones to avoid)

real trust signals:

- short quotes from real clients, with a name and a company.
- logos of businesses you have worked with, only with their permission.
- certifications you actually hold, with the issuing organisation named.
- a short "how i work" section: what happens after a client contacts you, how long a project takes, how revisions work.

fake trust signals to avoid:

- testimonials from people who never hired you.
- logos of companies you only applied to.
- numbers you cannot explain or verify.
- claims about experience you do not have.

fueler's guide [how to create a winning freelance portfolio](https://fueler.io/blog/how-to-create-a-winning-freelance-portfolio) covers social proof and process well: clients trust freelancers who show how they work, not just what they made.

## keeping it updated

a stale portfolio tells clients you have stopped caring. review it every two or three months:

- remove the weakest piece and add your best recent work.
- update your services and prices if they have changed.
- fix broken links and outdated contact details.
- add a new case study after every project you are proud of.

five minutes after finishing a project is the best time to update it, while the details are fresh. a current portfolio also protects you from one of the [common freelancing mistakes](/freelancing/common-freelancing-mistakes): letting your proof go stale while your skills move on.

![close-up of hands sketching a website layout wireframe in a paper notebook next to a laptop](/covers/freelance-case-study.jpg)

## frequently asked questions

### do i need a portfolio to start freelancing?

yes, in almost every field. clients need to see proof before they pay. three honest sample projects are enough to start. without any samples, you are asking clients to trust a promise.

### what should a freelance portfolio include?

your best three to twelve projects, short case studies explaining the problem and the result, a clear statement of who you help, your services, and an easy way to contact you. testimonials and a short "how i work" section help.

### where should i build my freelance portfolio?

a simple personal website is the best long-term home for it. portfolio builders are a fast start, and marketplace profiles are useful for being found. most freelancers use a personal site plus one marketplace profile.

### how do i make a portfolio with no experience?

create sample projects for imaginary or local businesses, label them clearly as samples, and present them with the same care as paid work. a good sample proves your skill; a fake client name destroys trust.

### how often should i update my portfolio?

every two to three months, or after every project you are proud of. remove weaker work as you add stronger work, so the portfolio always shows your current best.

## conclusion

a portfolio that gets you hired is short, specific, and honest. pick your best three to twelve projects, order them by the work you want more of, write a short case study for each, and put your services and contact details where a client can find them in seconds. if you have no clients yet, make three sample projects and label them as samples. then use your portfolio everywhere: in your marketplace profile, in your pitches, and in your social profiles. when it is live, the next step is putting it in front of people, which is exactly what our guide to [finding freelance clients](/freelancing/how-to-find-freelance-clients) covers. you can browse all of our [freelancing guides](/freelancing) for the full collection.

how to find freelance clients: 9 proven ways nine practical ways to find freelance clients, from your network and referrals to marketplaces, linkedin, and cold outreach, plus a system to track it all. freelancing clients marketing freelancing finding freelance clients is a skill, not luck. the freelancers with steady work do the same thing every week: they stay visible to people who already know them, and they reach out to people who need help right now. this guide explains nine proven ways to find freelance clients, in the order that works best for most beginners, plus a simple system to keep track of it all.

## before you look for clients: get the basics ready

clients check you before they reply. before you send a single message, make sure these three things exist:

- **one clear offer.** one sentence that says who you help and what you deliver, for example "i edit short videos for fitness coaches."
- **three samples.** a small [freelance portfolio](/freelancing/how-to-create-a-freelance-portfolio) that proves you can do the work, even if the samples are practice projects.
- **a way to contact you.** an email address or a simple contact form that you actually check every day.

without these, every channel below works worse. with them, even a short message can win work.

## 1. start with people who already know you

your first client is most likely someone who has seen your work before: a former manager, a colleague, a local business owner, or a friend who runs a small business. they already trust you, so you skip the hardest part of selling. if you are still setting up the basics, read our guide to [starting freelancing](/freelancing/how-to-start-freelancing) first, then come back here.

write a short, personal message to ten people. say what you offer, who it is for, and ask if they know anyone who needs it. do not send a mass message or a generic broadcast. one personal note each, mentioning something specific about them.

former employers are worth a message too. offer to take on a small overflow task or a one-off project. many companies prefer hiring a known freelancer over recruiting someone new.

## 2. ask for referrals

a happy client is the cheapest source of new clients. when a client praises your work at handover, ask one question: "do you know anyone else who might need help like this?" most clients are glad to introduce you, but almost none do it without being asked.

make it easy for them. send a short paragraph they can forward, describing what you do and who you help. offer the same courtesy in return: if you meet someone who needs a service you do not offer, pass them to a freelancer you trust.

referrals compound. one good client who introduces you to two more is worth more than fifty cold emails.

## 3. use marketplaces the smart way

marketplaces like upwork and fiverr bring clients to you, but they are crowded. use them selectively instead of applying to everything.

- **pick small, well-described jobs.** a job with a clear task, a realistic budget, and a client who has hired before is worth your time. vague jobs with no budget usually are not.
- **write the first two lines about the client.** name their problem and your solution before you talk about yourself. most proposals open with "i am a freelancer with five years of experience" and get skipped.
- **attach one relevant sample.** one sample that matches the job beats five unrelated ones.
- **apply consistently.** five thoughtful applications a week beats fifty copied ones.

check the platform's current fees and payment rules before you price work, because they change. if you have not worked out your prices yet, read our guide to [setting freelance rates](/freelancing/how-to-set-freelance-rates) first. upwork's own guide to [getting clients as a freelancer](https://www.upwork.com/resources/how-to-get-clients-as-a-freelancer) explains how proposals and profiles work on its platform.

## 4. use linkedin strategically

linkedin works for freelancers because clients search there when they need help, and because your posts reach people who already know you.

- rewrite your headline around the client's outcome, for example "landing pages for dental clinics" instead of "freelance designer".
- post once a week about your work: a finished project, a problem you solved, or a short tip in your niche. keep it practical, not promotional.
- comment on posts by founders and hiring managers in your niche. a useful comment is remembered; a sales pitch is ignored.
- when someone engages with your posts, send a short message. you are starting a conversation, not closing a sale.

## 5. send cold outreach that gets replies

cold outreach means contacting a business that has not asked for help. it works when the message is specific, short, and about them.

a message that gets replies has four parts:

1. one specific observation about their business ("your booking page still shows last month's schedule").
2. one sentence about what you can do ("i help small clinics clean up pages like that").
3. one small proof, such as a link to a sample or a one-line result.
4. one easy next step ("want me to send a quick example of how i would fix it?").

send ten of these a week to businesses that fit your niche, not a hundred generic emails. track every reply. if nobody answers after twenty messages, the problem is usually the offer or the targeting, not the volume.

## 6. find buying intent in public posts

some clients announce that they need help in public: hiring threads, community posts, and "looking for" messages on reddit, x, facebook groups, and niche forums. these leads are warm because the client is already looking.

look for posts with a clear task, a budget or rate range, a deadline, and contact instructions. avoid posts that promise "unlimited earning potential", ask you to pay to start, or refuse to explain the work.

score each lead before you pitch it. give one point for each of these:

| lead check | point if true |
|---|---|
| the task is clearly described | 1 |
| a budget or rate range is stated | 1 |
| the deadline is realistic | 1 |
| contact instructions are clear | 1 |
| you can show a relevant sample within a day | 1 |

pitch leads that score four or five. save three-point leads for later. skip the rest. a short guide to lead sources for beginners is the sidequestboard article [how to find freelance clients with no experience](https://www.sidequestboard.app/blog/how-to-find-freelance-clients-with-no-experience), which explains reddit hiring communities and beginner marketplace projects in detail.

![a laptop screen showing a simple spreadsheet list next to a notebook with handwritten notes](/covers/freelance-lead-scoring.jpg)

## 7. look for local businesses

local businesses are often overlooked by freelancers who only look online, and they are easier to understand. walk through your area, or search online maps, for businesses with a visible problem you can fix: a restaurant with an outdated menu, a clinic with an unclear services page, a shop with no social media posts for months.

lead with one small, helpful observation and one simple offer. do not send a message listing everything wrong with their business. one fix, clearly explained, is enough to start a conversation. local clients also tend to pay on time and refer you to other local businesses.

## 8. partner with other freelancers and agencies

you do not have to find every client yourself. partner with freelancers whose services complement yours: a web developer pairs with a designer, a writer pairs with an seo specialist, a video editor pairs with a social media manager. when one of you wins a project that needs the other's skill, you both earn.

small agencies are another source. many agencies hire freelancers for overflow work, and they pay faster than individual clients because they already have budgets. introduce yourself with a short message, your portfolio, and the type of work you want.

shopify's guide to [getting clients as a freelancer](https://www.shopify.com/sg/blog/how-to-get-clients-as-a-freelancer) covers partnerships, referrals, and owned channels in more depth.

## 9. build inbound: content and an email list

inbound means clients come to you. it is slow to start and powerful later. publish useful content about your niche once or twice a month: a short guide, a before-and-after case study, or a practical tip. share it where your clients spend time.

keep an email list of past clients, warm leads, and people who asked about your work. send a short update once a month: what you are working on, one useful tip, and whether you have availability. when a past client needs help again, your email is the reminder that brings them back.

![two professionals chatting over coffee at a bright coworking space with laptops on the table](/covers/freelance-networking.jpg)

## a weekly routine that finds clients

consistency beats intensity. a routine you can keep for months will find more clients than a frantic week of outreach followed by silence.

| day | task | target |
|---|---|---|
| monday | find new leads from marketplaces, communities, and local searches | 10 leads |
| tuesday | score the leads and pick the best five | 5 strong leads |
| wednesday | send personal pitches to the best leads | 5 pitches |
| thursday | follow up on last week's pitches, once each | all open leads |
| friday | post about your work and update your portfolio | 1 post, 1 improvement |

track everything in a simple spreadsheet: date, source, client, service needed, lead score, pitch sent, follow-up date, outcome. after a month you will see which channels actually bring replies, and you can spend more time there.

## how to follow up without being annoying

most freelancers never follow up, and most clients are simply busy. one polite follow-up a week after your first message is expected, not rude. keep it to two sentences: remind them what you offered and ask if the timing is better now. if there is still no reply after a second follow-up, move on. never send five messages to the same person.

## frequently asked questions

### how do i find freelance clients with no experience?

start with people who know you, then apply for small marketplace jobs with clear descriptions. build three honest sample projects first, so every pitch includes proof. public hiring posts and local businesses are good early sources because they judge the sample, not your resume.

### how many clients do i need?

it depends on your rates and your costs. three to five steady clients often provide more stability than twenty one-off jobs, because repeat clients need less selling and pay faster. aim for a mix: a few regular clients plus a small flow of new ones.

### should i work for free to get my first client?

a small, clearly limited sample or a discounted first project can be reasonable. open-ended free work is not. if a client asks for unpaid custom work before hiring, that is a warning sign. offer a small paid trial instead.

### how long does it take to find clients?

expect weeks of consistent outreach before the first replies, and longer before steady work. if you send five personal pitches a week and keep your portfolio updated, most beginners see results within one to three months.

### what is the best way to find clients as a freelancer?

there is no single best way. the freelancers with the steadiest work combine two or three channels: their network, one marketplace, and direct outreach or linkedin. relying on one channel alone leaves you exposed when it goes quiet.

## conclusion

finding clients is a weekly habit, not a one-time effort. start with the people who already know you, add one marketplace and one outreach channel, score your leads, and follow up once. keep a simple tracker so you learn what works. if you have not set up your proof yet, read our guide to [creating a freelance portfolio](/freelancing/how-to-create-a-freelance-portfolio) first, then come back and start with ten personal messages this week. and when you do land work, avoid the traps in our guide to [common freelancing mistakes](/freelancing/common-freelancing-mistakes). you can browse all of our [freelancing guides](/freelancing) for the full collection.

title: How to Start Freelancing: A Beginner's Guide
excerpt: Learn how to start freelancing step by step: pick a skill, choose a niche, build a portfolio, find your first clients, and set rates that pay your bills.

how to start freelancing: a beginner's guide learn how to start freelancing step by step: pick a skill, choose a niche, build a portfolio, find your first clients, and set rates that pay your bills. freelancing beginners getting started freelancing freelancing means selling a skill directly to clients, usually one project at a time, instead of working for a single employer. you choose the work, set your schedule, and get paid per project or per hour. this guide shows you how to start freelancing from zero: how to pick a service, check that people will pay for it, build proof you can do the work, and land your first paying client.

## what freelancing actually is (and what it is not)

a freelancer is a self-employed person who sells services to several clients. writers, designers, developers, video editors, virtual assistants, marketers, translators, and bookkeepers all freelance. you are your own boss, but you are also your own sales team, accountant, and customer support.

freelancing is not passive income. you earn when you deliver work, and you spend unpaid time finding clients, writing proposals, invoicing, and learning. it is also not a shortcut around learning a skill. clients pay for results, so the skill comes first and the business comes second.

the honest version of the timeline: most beginners take weeks to a few months to land a first paid project, and longer to reach steady income. anyone promising first-week riches is selling a course, not a career.

## step 1: pick one skill you can sell

start with what you can already do, or what you can learn to a usable standard in a few weeks of focused practice. good first services are specific and easy to explain: writing blog posts, designing social media graphics, editing short videos, building simple websites, managing a small business inbox, or setting up spreadsheets.

ask yourself three questions:

- what have people already paid me for, praised me for, or asked me to help with?
- can i deliver this to a professional standard, even if slowly?
- can i show it? a skill you cannot demonstrate is hard to sell.

if you are choosing between two skills, pick the one with clearer buyers. a general skill like "digital marketing" is hard to sell; a specific one like "email newsletters for online shops" is easy to explain and easy to buy.

avoid starting with five services at once. one clear offer makes your profile, portfolio, and pitches ten times easier to write.

## step 2: check the demand before you commit

before you spend a month learning, check that clients are actually hiring for your skill.

- search freelance marketplaces for your service and read real job posts. note the words clients use, the budgets they mention, and how many proposals each job gets.
- search for the service on google and linkedin. if businesses are advertising for it, demand exists.
- look at what successful freelancers in that skill charge and how they describe their work. you are researching the market, not copying their profiles.

if you find almost no job posts, the skill may be too new, too narrow, or described with different words. try the closest related terms before giving up on it.

## step 3: choose a niche

a niche is a specific type of client plus a specific problem you solve. "i write" is a service. "i write product descriptions for small skincare brands" is a niche. clients hire specialists because specialists feel safer than generalists.

| niche example | who the client is | what you deliver |
|---|---|---|
| landing pages for dentists | local dental clinics | one page, booking form, clear services |
| short video editing for coaches | fitness and business coaches | reels and shorts from long videos |
| blog posts for saas companies | small software teams | one researched article per week |
| bookkeeping for online shops | ecommerce sellers | monthly records and simple reports |

pick a niche where you understand the client's world. if you have worked in hospitality, restaurants and hotels are a natural first niche. if you studied finance, small business bookkeeping is. your background is an advantage, not a limitation.

your niche can change later. it is a starting point, not a life sentence.

![a person writing ideas on sticky notes on a bright home office wall](/covers/freelance-choose-skill.jpg)

## step 4: build a small portfolio with no clients

you do not need paid work to prove you can do the work. you need three to five honest samples. create them as practice projects and label them clearly as samples.

ideas that work for common skills:

- **writing:** publish two sample articles on a free blog or a document anyone can open. write about a real topic, not about yourself.
- **design:** redesign a local business logo, menu, or social media post, and show the before and after.
- **video:** edit three short clips from free stock footage and show the finished result.
- **development:** build one simple website for an imaginary business and put it online.
- **virtual assistance:** create a sample inbox system, a formatted spreadsheet, or a tidy notion workspace and record a short walkthrough.

for each sample, write three short lines: what the client needed, what you did, and what the result was. if the work is a sample, say so. inventing clients or results destroys trust the moment a real client asks a follow-up question.

our full guide to [creating a freelance portfolio](/freelancing/how-to-create-a-freelance-portfolio) covers sample projects, case studies, and where to host your portfolio.

## step 5: set up your profiles

you need one place clients can find you and one place you can send them.

- **one marketplace profile.** upwork suits most skills; fiverr suits packaged services with fixed prices. pick one, fill it in completely, and use a clear headline that names your service and your client, for example "blog writer for saas companies" instead of "freelance writer".
- **one portfolio page.** a single page with your best samples, a short introduction, your services, and a contact button is enough. link it from every profile.
- **one professional social profile.** linkedin works for most business services. keep the headline client focused and post about your work once a week.

use the same photo, headline, and description everywhere. consistency makes you look established even when you are new.

## step 6: find your first clients

your first client is most likely someone who already knows your work: a former colleague, a local business owner, or a friend of a friend. tell ten people, in person, that you are taking on freelance work and exactly what you offer. most beginners skip this step and wonder why nobody finds them.

after that, work through the channels in order:

1. your network and former employers.
2. one marketplace, applying to small jobs with clear descriptions.
3. direct outreach to businesses that visibly need your service.
4. communities where your clients spend time, such as industry groups and forums.

our guide to [finding freelance clients](/freelancing/how-to-find-freelance-clients) explains each channel in detail, including how to score leads and what to write in your first message.

## step 7: set your first rate

do not copy your old hourly wage. as a freelancer you pay your own taxes, insurance, software, and unpaid time, so your rate has to be higher than an employee wage for the same work. a simple starting method: work out what you need to earn each month, add your business costs, and divide by the hours you can realistically bill (usually 20 to 25 a week, not 40).

start at a rate you can defend, not the lowest rate you can survive on. low rates attract the hardest clients and leave no room to grow. read our guide to [setting freelance rates](/freelancing/how-to-set-freelance-rates) for the full calculation, pricing models, and a worked example.

## step 8: get the admin right

three small habits prevent most beginner disasters:

- **use a written agreement for every project.** scope, deliverables, deadlines, payment terms, and revision limits, even in a one-page document. verbal agreements lead to disputes.
- **ask for a deposit.** a 30 to 50 percent upfront payment is normal for direct clients and protects you from non-payment.
- **track your money from day one.** keep a separate record of income and expenses, and set aside a portion of every payment for tax. the exact portion depends on where you live, so check your local tax rules early.

keep your business records in one place: contracts, invoices, receipts, and client contact details. ten minutes of admin per project saves hours of confusion later.

## your first 30 days: a simple plan

![a paper wall calendar and a handwritten checklist on a wooden desk with a pen and a laptop nearby](/covers/freelance-first-30-days.jpg)

| week | focus | done when |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | choose one service and one niche | you can describe your offer in one sentence |
| 2 | build three portfolio samples | samples are live and shareable |
| 3 | set up one marketplace profile and one portfolio page | a stranger can understand what you sell in ten seconds |
| 4 | contact ten people and apply to five suitable jobs | every message is personal, not copied and pasted |

if nobody replies in the first month, change one thing at a time: the niche, the samples, or the message. do not change everything at once, or you will never know what worked.

## mistakes to avoid at the start

- offering every service to every client. specialists get hired; generalists get ignored.
- waiting until you feel ready. you will never feel ready. start with a small project you can deliver well.
- working without a contract or a deposit.
- copying another freelancer's rates without checking your own costs.
- spending a month on a logo and a website before talking to a single client.

we cover all of these in detail in [common freelancing mistakes to avoid](/freelancing/common-freelancing-mistakes).

## frequently asked questions

### can i start freelancing with no experience?

yes, if you can show the work. build three honest sample projects, label them as samples, and apply for small jobs that match them. clients hire proof, not years on a resume.

### do i need a degree to freelance?

no. clients care about your samples, your communication, and whether you deliver on time. a degree can help in regulated fields such as law or accounting, but for most freelance services it is not required.

### how long does it take to get the first client?

it varies. beginners with a clear offer and a portfolio often land a first small project within a few weeks to a few months. it takes longer if the offer is vague, the portfolio is empty, or you only apply to a handful of jobs.

### should i quit my job to start freelancing?

not at first. start on the side, build a few clients and a small income buffer, and only consider going full time when your freelance income is steady. a common benchmark is covering a large share of your current salary for several months in a row.

### which freelance platform is best for beginners?

it depends on your service. upwork works well for most professional services and longer projects. fiverr works well for packaged services with a fixed price. pick one, learn how it works, and focus there instead of spreading yourself across five platforms.

## conclusion

starting freelancing comes down to a short sequence: pick one skill, narrow it to a niche, prove it with three honest samples, tell people you are available, and price your work to cover your real costs. do those five things well and the rest is practice. for the next step, read our guide to [finding freelance clients](/freelancing/how-to-find-freelance-clients) and start with the ten people who already know your work. you can browse all of our [freelancing guides](/freelancing) for the full collection.
